title: Grain Whisky Versus Neutral Spirit | Craft Beer School
desc: What separates grain whisky from neutral spirit in distillation strength, maturation and flavour and why it matters for Indian whisky labels.
teaser: Both come from grain and column stills. One keeps its flavour and must age in oak. The other is stripped almost bare.
standfirst: Grain whisky and neutral spirit can start from the same maize or wheat and run through similar column stills. The difference is how far the distiller pushes the strength and what happens afterwards. That difference decides whether the result can be called whisky.
sections:
Grain whisky is usually made from wheat or maize, with a share of malted barley to supply enzymes. It is distilled in a continuous column still, often a Coffey still, the design patented by Aeneas Coffey in 1830. Neutral spirit can come from the same grains or from molasses. It is also made in column stills.

The split happens in how the still is run. Grain whisky is distilled to a strength that leaves some flavour behind. Neutral spirit is rectified until almost nothing but ethanol and water remains. Our guide to malt, grain and blended whisky places grain whisky in the family.

Scotch rules and EU rules require whisky to be distilled to less than 94.8% ABV, so that it keeps the aroma and taste of the raw materials. Grain whisky in Scotland is typically distilled close to that limit, but below it.

Neutral spirit is distilled higher, often around 96% ABV, approaching the limit that simple distillation of ethanol and water can reach. At that strength most congeners, the flavour compounds such as higher alcohols, esters and aldehydes, have been separated out. What remains is close to tasteless apart from the alcohol.

A point or so of strength sounds small. In flavour terms it is a big gap, because the last stages of rectification are exactly where the remaining congeners are removed.

Grain whisky must then be matured like any other Scotch: at least three years in oak casks in Scotland. It picks up colour, vanilla, coconut and sweetness from the wood. Mature grain whisky can be light but distinctly flavoured. Some is bottled on its own as single grain whisky, meaning grain whisky from a single distillery. Our guide to how whisky is made covers maturation.

Neutral spirit needs no maturation. It is used as the base for vodka, gin, liqueurs and many other drinks.

Many Indian whiskies are blends that include neutral spirit, often extra neutral alcohol (ENA) made from molasses or grain, combined with some malt or grain whisky and flavourings. Under Scotch or EU rules such a blend would not qualify as whisky. Under Indian standards and state rules it can be sold as whisky, depending on the current notification.

For a craft distillery this is a strategic choice. A product built entirely from grain and malt whisky, distilled below 94.8% and matured in oak, can be sold in strict export markets. A product with molasses ENA usually cannot. Our guide to molasses versus grain spirit in India explains the background.
Running a column for grain whisky

Making grain whisky in a column still means deliberately not chasing maximum strength. The distiller controls reflux and draws the spirit at a point that keeps some congeners. Too high and the spirit is close to neutral. Too low and heavy fusel oils come through.

The floor detail we would insist on: log draw strength continuously and alarm on it, not just at shift end. A column drifting from 94% towards 96% in the small hours is quietly making neutral spirit. In a strict market that batch is no longer whisky.

New make grain whisky is lighter than malt new make, with sweet cereal, light fruit and a solvent edge that settles with age. Maize tends to give sweeter, rounder notes. Wheat tends to give softer, creamier ones. After years in oak, the cask plays a large part in the final flavour, often more than in a heavier malt.

That lightness is why grain whisky forms the bulk of many blends. It carries the flavour of the malts and the casks without competing too hard.

Write your strength, grain and maturation rules into your product specification before you design the plant. A column still capable of neutral spirit can also make grain whisky, but only if it is run that way and the records prove it. Understanding the chemistry of rectification and how it shapes flavour is part of a distilling course rather than a footnote.

Your first step: check the draw strength logs from your last ten column runs and mark any that went above 94.8%.
faqs: What is the difference between grain whisky and neutral spirit?
Grain whisky is distilled below 94.8% ABV to keep some flavour and is matured in oak. Neutral spirit is rectified higher, often around 96%, until it is close to flavourless. It needs no maturation.
Is grain whisky made in column stills?
Usually yes, typically in continuous column stills such as the Coffey still, run so the spirit keeps some congeners.
Not under Scotch or EU rules. Indian standards and state rules can allow blends with neutral spirit to be sold as whisky, depending on the current notification.
Grain whisky from a single distillery, often bottled on its own rather than used in a blend.
